stories.title: Ethiopia: El Niño, Iran War Shocks Could Push Nearly One Million More Ethiopians Into Poverty, New Report Warns
stories.summary: Ethiopia: El NiÃ±o, Iran War Shocks Could Push Nearly One Million More Ethiopians Into Poverty, New Report Warns 18 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Nearly 905,000 additional people in Ethiopia could be pushed into poverty and 2.8 million into undernourishment in 2027 as the effects of a potentially exceptionally strong El Niño converge with higher global fuel prices linked to the Iran war, according to a new analysis by the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI). The analysis, published on November 17 by IFPRI researchers Emerta Aragie and Chris Hillbruner, projects that the combined shocks could reduce Ethiopia's gross domestic product (GDP) by between 0.4% and 1.1% below its projected baseline, with an average decline of 0.8%. Agriculture is expected to bear a disproportionate share of the economic damage, with agricultural GDP projected to contract by 2% in the average scenario. The researchers identified El Niño-related agricultural losses as the principal driver of the projected economic slowdown. However, higher global fuel prices associated with disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz are also expected to compound pressure on household incomes, purchasing power and food security.

The resolution, which seeks to amend the constitution, now requires President Bola Tinubu's assent to become law. Its latest findings point to the growing role of drones in the war, with attacks increasingly reaching beyond the front lines to strike markets, hospitals, schools, and infrastructure essential to civilian survival. The UN Human Rights Office has confirmed that at least 2,230 civilians were killed in Sudan between January and October, more than 1,630 of them in drone strikes. A report released today says more than 1,390 civilians were killed during the first six months of 2026 in the conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), and allied armed movements. More than 80 per cent of these deaths resulted from drone strikes, which have become a defining feature of the war.

As external financing becomes increasingly uncertain and public health emergencies continue to test health systems, African countries are strengthening the institutions, capabilities and partnerships needed to take greater ownership of their health future. stories.title: Sudan: Bishops Call for Peace As War Spreads
stories.summary: Sudan: Bishops Call for Peace As War Spreads 18 November 2026 Fides News Agency (Vatican) Khartoum — "We appeal to the African Union, the United Nations, IGAD (Intergovernmental Authority on Development), the Holy See and the international communities to intensify coordinated diplomatic efforts towards immediate cessation of hostilities, inclusive dialogue and restoration of peace in Sudan." This is the appeal issued by the Bishops of Sudan and South Sudan in the concluding statement of their Plenary Assembly, held in Juba, South Sudan, from November 7 to 14, (see Fides, 17/11/2026). Sudan has been ravaged by more than three years of war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group commanded by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo. The conflict broke out on April 15, 2023, following a power struggle over control of the country and disagreements over plans to integrate the RSF into the national army (see Fides, 17/4/2023). In their statement, the Bishops also express concern over "threats against Christian communities, clergy and church institutions in Sudan", although they do not cite specific incidents. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Since the beginning of the year, 2,230 civilians have been killed in Sudan, according to figures released yesterday, November 17, by the United Nations Human Rights Office.

stories.title: Djibouti: Six Survivors Reach Berbera Port After Boat Sailing From Djibouti Sinks
stories.summary: Djibouti: Six Survivors Reach Berbera Port After Boat Sailing From Djibouti Sinks 17 November 2026 Horn Diplomat (Hargeisa) By Mohamed Duale Berbera — Six crew members rescued after a cargo boat sank near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait have arrived safely at Somaliland's Berbera Port, where medical personnel and emergency teams are providing care, the Somaliland Ports Authority said on Tuesday. Two other crew members died when the boat, Alfatah, sank on Nov. 16 while carrying cooking oil from Djibouti to Yemen's Salif Port, the authority said in a statement. The survivors were rescued by M/V Adel 2 and brought to Berbera, where port teams received them and provided medical attention and emergency assistance. "Six crew members rescued by M/V Adel 2 following the sinking of the boat Alfatah near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait on 16 November 2026 have safely arrived at Berbera Port," the authority said. Eight crew members were aboard Alfatah when it sank. The six survivors comprise two Yemeni, two Somali and two Indian nationals.

Sur les 2230 civils tués entre début janvier et fin octobre confirmés par le Haut Commissariat des Nations unies aux droits de l'homme, plus de 1630 ont été tués lors d'attaques de drones, qui ont « éclipsé l'usage d'autres tactiques et armements », a-t-il précisé. Publié le : 17/11/2026 - 09:11 Modifié le : 17/11/2026 - 10:08 2 min Temps de lecture Des responsables de l'administration locale se rendent sur un marché après une attaque présumée de drone, dans un lieu situé dans la région d'Abyei, le long de la frontière entre le Soudan du Sud et le Soudan, le 20 octobre 2026, comme le montre cette capture d'écran tirée d'une vidéo fournie par l'agence. via REUTERS - Radio Tamazuj Par : RFI avec AFP Publicité Lire la suite C’est une tendance lourde qui se confirme de semaine en semaine au Soudan , pays en proie à une violente guerre qui oppose depuis avril 2023 l’armée régulière du général Abdel Fattah al-Burhan à son ex-allié le général Mohamed Hamdan Dogolo « Hemedti » et ses Forces de soutien rapide (FSR) : près des trois quarts des morts de civils répertoriées en 2026 sont liées à des frappes de drones. Le Haut-Commissariat des Nations unies aux droits de l'homme (HCDH) a cependant souligné que le bilan total de ces victimes civiles des derniers mois est probablement plus élevé. Les travailleurs humanitaires estiment que la guerre entre les Forces armées soudanaises et les paramilitaires a fait plus de 200 000 morts au total.

Photograph: K Desouki/AFP/Getty ‘I’m not ready to go to jail’: co-founder of Egypt’s last independent media outlet faces prison Mada Masr, the news site co-founded by Lina Attalah just before the 2013 military coup, is fighting for its life after being shut down, but its journalists have not given up hope F acing a year in prison for running Egypt’s leading independent news outlet Mada Masr , Lina Attalah is trying to focus on the everyday: waking at dawn to hear the birds sing before Cairo’s streets come alive and visiting Mada Masr’s shuttered offices with her reporters to water the plants and feed their four cats. Attalah is the reluctant face of Egypt’s embattled independent press at a moment of crisis. stories.title: Guinée: 22 ex-administrateurs territoriaux condamnés à deux ans de prison dans l'affaire d'orpaillage illégal à Siguiri
stories.summary: Guinée: 22 ex-administrateurs territoriaux condamnés à deux ans de prison dans l'affaire d'orpaillage illégal à Siguiri Jugés devant la Cour de répression des infractions économiques et financières (Crief) pour leur complicité présumée dans l'exploitation minière clandestine qui a débouché sur une catastrophe écologique à Siguiri, ils ont été reconnus coupables de complicité de dégradation de l'environnement, destructions diverses et pollution des eaux. Les 202 orpailleurs également poursuivis dans ce dossier ont quant à eux été condamnés à trois ans de prison et à une amende solidaire de 10 milliards de francs guinéens. Publié le : 17/11/2026 - 04:40 2 min Temps de lecture Les ex-administrateurs territoriaux (en orange) de la région de Siguiri et, derrière eux, les 202 orpailleurs également poursuivis dans ce dossier lors d'une audience devant la Crief, le 11 novembre dernier, à Conakry. © Mouctar Bah / RFI Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Avec notre correspondant à Conakry, Mouctar Bah Le verdict est tombé au procès des 224 individus poursuivis devant la Cour de répression des infractions économiques et financières (Crief) dans le cadre de l'affaire de l'exploitation minière clandestine de Siguiri qui a débouché sur un désastre écologique, dans le nord-est du pays, lundi 16 novembre. Les 202 orpailleurs reconnus coupables d'exploitation illégale de substances minières et d'atteinte à l’environnement ont été condamnés à trois ans de prison assortis d'une amende solidaire de 10 milliards de francs guinéens - l'équivalent d'environ un million d’euros - et de 10 ans d'interdiction de séjour en Guinée pour les ressortissants étrangers concernés. Quant aux 22 anciens administrateurs territoriaux eux aussi dans le collimateur de la justice, s'ils ont été relaxés des accusations de corruption, d'enrichissement illicite et de blanchiment de capitaux, ils écopent chacun en revanche de deux ans de prison ferme et d'une amende de 10 millions de francs guinéens pour complicité de dégradation de l'environnement, destructions diverses et pollution des eaux.

Photograph: Leonhard Föger/Reuters Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’ Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”. The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country. In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school. "Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says. One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village. "They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says. stories.title: Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
stories.summary: Image source, Reuters By Olivia Ireland Â and Â Bethany Bell ,Â Reporting from Vienna Published 16 November 2026 Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals. Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements. The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin. Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said. The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed.

stories.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5PRq5 Prefer DW on Google Nigeria's 2027 general election will take place against the backdrop of AI-driven disinformation Image: Adekunle Ajayi/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis . He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi. The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI) . Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died. The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election.

Ten minutes later on the evening of 18 October, a second drone hit the same site in the town in West Kordofan state, Sudan . At least 139 people were killed. stories.title: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Pro-government forces marched into Tigray's capital less than two weeks after the war began By Michael Teferi ,Â BBC Africa Â and Â Yemane Nagish ,Â BBC Tigrinya Published 13 November 2026 Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment. "People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC. After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter. "Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion. Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next." Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022.

stories.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
stories.summary: ‘I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey’ … Simbarashe Kundizeza View image in fullscreen ‘I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey’ … Simbarashe Kundizeza Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’ The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation. Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter , which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October. Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement : “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.” She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation. “Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.” Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.

stories.title: Can Nigeria's president regain voters' trust after painful first term?
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, President Tinubu faces re-election with the cost of living and economic hardship the major issues for many voters By Ondiro Oganga Published 12 November 2026 Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages. The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes. Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs. Nigeria is due to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar among Tinubu's main challengers. The manifesto, launched on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), reflects the government's bid to win back the trust of Nigerians.
